text: You're given a list of intervals, in no particular order, and some of them overlap. Merge all the overlapping ones and return a list of non-overlapping intervals that covers exactly the same points.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if two intervals only touch, like one to four and four to five, should they merge? And does the output need to be in any order?
Touching intervals merge, so that's one to five. Any order is fine, but sorted is natural.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: if I sort by start, an interval can only overlap the last group I've built. Every earlier group ended before the last group started, so it ends before the current start too. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Between one and ten to the fourth intervals, and values from zero to ten to the fourth.

Got it. At least one interval, so I can seed the result with the first one. Let me check the examples. One to three and two to six overlap, so one to six; eight to ten and fifteen to eighteen stay alone. Second example, one to four and four to five touch, so one to five. Both match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would compare every pair and merge until nothing changes. That's at least quadratic, and one merge can create new overlaps, so it repeats. I could also mark every covered point on a number line, but then the speed depends on the coordinate range. This problem reminds me of a sort-then-sweep pattern. Once the intervals are sorted by start, a single left-to-right pass is enough, because only the newest group can still grow.
Are you confident the single pass is correct?

Yes. The invariant is that after each step, my result is the merge of everything seen so far, sorted and non-overlapping. A new interval either reaches the last group, so I extend it, or starts after it, so it opens a new group. I also checked it against the number-line version: every list of up to four intervals on coordinates zero to five, about two hundred thousand cases, plus twenty thousand random ones. Zero mismatches.

Here's the plan, in three steps. Sort by start. Put the first interval in the result. Then for each next interval, if the last group's end reaches its start, extend that end to the larger of the two; otherwise push it as a new group. One thing worth flagging — compare against the last group in the result, not the previous input interval, and always take the max for the end.

Alright. Sort, seed the result with the first interval, then one loop. If the result's last end is greater than or equal to the current start, I set that end to the max of the two. Otherwise I push the current interval. The easy line to get wrong is that max. Sorting only orders the starts; ends can go down. With one to ten followed by two to three, a plain assignment shrinks the group to one to three. And both official examples still pass with that bug, because neither has an interval inside another.

Let's dry-run an unsorted case: eight to ten, one to nine, three to four, twelve to thirteen, two to six. Expected one to ten and twelve to thirteen. After sorting, one to nine swallows two to six and three to four, and the end stays at nine thanks to the max. The moment that matters is eight to ten: nine reaches eight, so the group grows to ten. Then twelve is past ten, so a new group. Corner cases: a single interval comes back as is. All identical intervals become one. Nested intervals collapse into the outer one. Disjoint points stay separate.

Let me think about complexity here. Sorting is n log n, and the loop is linear, so time is n log n. Space is linear for the output, plus the sort's recursion. If the values are small, like here, I could bucket by start and skip the comparison sort, but the sorted version is the general answer.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why, after sorting, only the last group can change, which is the whole reason one pass works. You flagged the max on the end and showed a nested case the examples don't cover. And you knew the sort is the real cost, and when you could avoid it. Good work.
